name: tide
summary: Every piece paints the cell it stops on in your colour, and the other side can paint it back the same way.
After sixty turns each, whoever has more cells in their colour wins; equal counts draw.
Waves step to either cell ahead or to the side; surges run up to three cells straight ahead; leapers jump two cells diagonally, any way, over anything.
Only the leaper can turn back: everything else flows toward the far side.
Land on an enemy piece to take it. It joins your hand, and instead of moving you may set it down on any empty cell of your own half, painting that cell.
If you ever have no move at all, you lose.
description: A fight for ground in which nothing stays claimed. Every move paints the cell it ends on, and an enemy piece that later lands there paints it back, so the colours in the middle of the game are only a promise: what counts is the colour when the sixty turns run out. What stops this from becoming an endless trade of the same few cells is that the armies cannot go home. Waves and surges only ever move ahead or, for a wave, sideways, so every forward step is road a piece will never travel again, and every cell it leaves behind is one it can no longer defend. Each turn asks whether to spend a piece now or keep it in reserve. Pushed into the opponent's half, it paints cells they must come back for, but it can be taken by the pieces still waiting there and it can never come back to help. Held at home, it guards your ground and keeps a move in hand. Taking a piece paints its cell and puts the piece in your hand, and a held piece can be set down on any empty cell of your own half. That makes the hand a second reserve: drop it early as a fresh piece, or keep it for the last turns to win back cells an enemy raider has painted. The leaper, the one piece that can turn round, is the surest way to hunt raiders behind your lines, since a wave can only reach one that stands beside it. Push everything and you run out of moves, which loses outright. Hold everything back and the opponent paints the middle and much of your side. A typical game opens with both sides painting their own half, meets in a long exchange across the middle, and ends with surges spent on the far rows, leapers hunting, and held pieces set down on cells the raiders took.
